Chapter 8: Sustaining Progress and Preventing Regression
You know, training really isn’t a one-and-done thing. It’s more like a lifelong journey you share with your dog—a partnership that grows and changes over time. So, how do you keep making progress and make sure you don’t slide backwards? Let’s dig into some ways you can both stay engaged, keep building on what you’ve learned, and actually enjoy the process along the way.
Here’s something that’s easy to overlook—maintenance. Think about any skill you’ve learned, whether it’s playing an instrument or riding a bike. If you stop practicing, things start to slip, right? It’s the same with your dog’s training. Skills fade if you don’t use them, especially when new distractions pop up or life gets a little unpredictable.
That’s why it helps to weave training into your everyday routine. Instead of waiting for a perfect block of time for a formal session, try slipping in short, playful practice moments as you go about your day. Maybe you toss in a quick retrieve during a walk, or ask for a bit of steadiness while you’re at home. Even changing up the setting now and then—like practicing in a new park or a different room—can keep things interesting and help your dog get used to handling surprises.
Variety really is the spice of life, for both you and your dog. Mixing up the kinds of retrieves, new locations, or even adding little challenges keeps your training fresh and fun. Plus, it helps your dog learn to handle new situations with confidence—so when something unexpected happens, you’re both ready for it.
Here’s another thing that makes a big difference: celebrating progress. It’s so easy to focus on what still needs work, but every little win counts. Maybe your dog finally nails that tricky recall or stays steady when the doorbell rings. Take a moment to notice those milestones—big or small—and let your dog know you’re proud. That encouragement builds your bond and keeps both of you motivated.
Now, let’s be real—setbacks happen. Life changes, schedules shift, or maybe there’s a break in training because of travel or health. The important thing is to stay observant. Notice if your dog seems less enthusiastic, or if certain skills aren’t as sharp. When that happens, don’t stress—just go back to basics for a bit, and give yourselves time to get back on track. Patience and flexibility here are your best friends.
So, what habits can gently keep you moving forward? Here’s a quick list to keep in mind:
First, fold training into your daily routine. That way, it never feels like a chore, and your dog’s skills stay sharp. Second, switch up your exercises and the places you train so things stay fresh and your dog learns to adapt. Third, don’t forget to celebrate those achievements, no matter how small—they all count. Fourth, keep an eye out for any signs your dog might be slipping and respond calmly, with a little extra patience. And finally, remind yourself that this is a lifelong journey for both of you. Treat it as a partnership with lots of chances to learn and grow together.
When you think of training as an ongoing journey, you create space for both you and your dog to keep improving, adapting, and—most importantly—enjoying the adventure you share. Here’s to many more years of working, learning, and having fun together.
